title: Buoyancy
summary: Archimedes' principle, floating and sinking, ships, hydrometers, and balloons.
cards.0.h: Where does the buoyant force come from?
cards.0.p: The bottom face of a submerged object is deeper. So the push from below is larger than the push from above. The forces on the sides cancel. The difference is the upward buoyant force (Fb).
cards.0.key: If liquid cannot get under the object (it is stuck to the bottom), there is no buoyant force.
cards.1.p: By Archimedes' principle, the buoyant force equals the weight of the liquid the object displaces. It is given by Fb = Vsub·ρliq·g (g ≈ 10 m/s²).
cards.1.key: V<sub>sub</sub> is not the whole volume of the object. It is the volume of the part that is in the liquid.
cards.1.once.soru: An object with 200 cm³ under water displaces 200 cm³ of water. This water weighs 2 N. What is the buoyant force on the object, in N?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: The buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced liquid. This is Archimedes' principle.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: A liquid exerts a buoyant force on every object submerged in it.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: 200 cm³ of water is 0.2 kg, and it weighs 2 N.
cards.2.h: Weighing in air and in a liquid
cards.2.p: In air a spring scale shows the weight of the object (W). In water the reading drops, because the buoyant force pushes the object up. This new reading is called the apparent weight, and it equals W − Fb.
cards.2.key: This stone has a volume of 200 cm³ and a mass of 500 g. Its density is 500 / 200 = 2.5 g/cm³.
cards.3.h: What changes as you go deeper?
cards.3.p: When a fully submerged object goes deeper, the pressures on its top and bottom faces increase by the same amount. The difference, F<sub>b</sub>, stays constant. If a partly submerged object is pushed down, F<sub>b</sub> increases.
cards.3.key: The density of the liquid is assumed not to change with depth.
cards.4.p: If ρobj < ρliq the object floats, and if they are equal it stays suspended. In both cases Fb = W. If the density of the object is higher, it sinks. Then Fb < W, and the bottom carries the difference.
cards.4.key: A suspended object can stay at any depth in the liquid and does not touch the bottom.
cards.4.once.soru: Wood with a density of 0.6 g/cm³ and iron with 7.8 g/cm³ are put in water (1 g/cm³). Which one floats?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: What is less dense than water floats, and what is denser sinks. With equal densities it would stay suspended.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: Iron is about 8 times denser than water, so it sinks.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: Iron is denser than water, so it cannot float.
cards.5.h: How deep does a floating object sit?
cards.5.p: For a floating object, Fb = W gives Vsub / V = ρobj / ρliq. The density of ice is about 0.9 g/cm³. So nine tenths of the ice stays under water.
cards.5.key: When ice floating in fresh water melts, the water level does not change. The meltwater exactly fills the submerged volume of the ice.
cards.5.etk.soru: Change the density of the object and of the liquid. How much of the object is submerged?
cards.5.etk.yorum.0.1: The object floats. F<sub>b</sub> = W, and part of the object stays out of the liquid.
cards.5.etk.yorum.1.1: The object stays suspended. It is fully submerged, and F<sub>b</sub> = W.
cards.5.etk.yorum.2.1: The object sinks. F<sub>b</sub> < W, and the object rests on the bottom.
cards.6.p: For a submerged cork tied to the bottom by a string, Fb = W + T. For a stone hanging from a string and lowered into water, T + Fb = W. Here T is the apparent weight.
cards.6.key: T is the tension in the string.
cards.6.once.soru: A cork tied to the bottom by a string is fully under water. The string is taut. What happens if you cut the string?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: The buoyant force is larger than the weight. The string was holding the difference, so F<sub>b</sub> = W + T.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: The string is taut, so it was pulling the cork down.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: Cork is less dense than water. So it rises when the string is cut.
cards.7.h: At the boundary of two liquids
cards.7.p: An object at the boundary of two liquids that do not mix gets a buoyant force from both. It is given by Fb = V₁·ρ₁·g + V₂·ρ₂·g. At equilibrium Fb = W.
cards.7.once.soru: A cube rests in equilibrium half in water (1 g/cm³) and half in the oil above (0.8 g/cm³). What is the density of the cube?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: The object gets a buoyant force from both liquids. If it sits half in each, its density is the average of the two: (1 + 0.8) / 2 = 0.9.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: Then it would stay suspended entirely in the water.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: Then it would stay suspended in the oil.
cards.8.p: Steel sinks, but a ship floats. The reason is that a ship is a shell full of air, and its average density is lower than water's. A loaded ship sits deeper.
cards.8.svg#5: a ship is a shell full of air: low average ρ
cards.8.key: For a floating ship F<sub>b</sub> = W<sub>ship</sub> + W<sub>load</sub>.
cards.9.p: A hydrometer is a glass float with a heavy bottom, and in every liquid Fb = W. It sinks less in a dense liquid and more in a thin one. The density is read from the mark on its stem.
cards.9.key: The scale increases downward. In a dense liquid the surface meets the lower marks on the stem.
cards.9.once.soru: You put a glass rod that floats in any liquid first in salt water, then in fresh water. In which one does it sink deeper?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: For a floating object F<sub>b</sub> = W is constant. Fresh water is less dense, so the object must sink deeper to get the same buoyant force.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: Salt water is denser. The same force is reached with less sinking.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: The liquids have different densities, so the submerged volume is different too.
cards.10.p: Air is a fluid too, and it exerts a buoyant force on objects in it. Helium (about 0.17 kg/m³) is less dense than air (about 1.2 kg/m³). That is why a balloon rises. Hot air also becomes less dense and rises.
cards.10.key: 1 m³ of helium gets a buoyant force of about 12 N, and its own weight is about 1.7 N. The net lift is about 10 N.
cards.11.h: The overflow can and the scale
cards.11.p: A full overflow can spills as much liquid as the submerged volume of the object. The weight of the spilled liquid equals Fb. In a container that does not overflow, an object raises the scale reading by W. If the object hangs from a string, the increase is Fb.
cards.11.key: In a full overflow can a floating object does not change the scale reading. A sinking object raises it by W − F<sub>b</sub>.
cards.11.once.soru: You drop a stone into an overflow can filled to the brim, and the stone sinks. What does the weight of the spilled water equal?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: The spilled water equals the submerged volume of the stone. By Archimedes' principle the weight of this water equals the buoyant force.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: The stone sank, so its weight is larger than the buoyant force. The spilled water is lighter than the stone.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: The weight of the can does not change. The spilled water depends only on the submerged volume of the stone.
cards.12.p:
• The buoyant force is Fb = Vsub·ρliq·g, and it comes from a pressure difference.
• The apparent weight is W − Fb.
• For floating and suspended objects Fb = W.
• For a fully submerged object, depth does not change Fb.
• Gases exert a buoyant force too.
quiz.0.q: A stone reads 12 N on a spring scale in air and 8 N when fully submerged in water. If the density of water is 1 g/cm³ and g = 10 m/s², what is the density of the stone, in g/cm³?
quiz.0.e: Since F<sub>b</sub> = 12 − 8 = 4 N, V = 400 cm³. The mass is 1.2 kg, or 1200 g, so ρ = 1200 / 400 = 3 g/cm³.
quiz.1.q: The objects are put in water (ρ = 1 g/cm³). Choose what each one does.
quiz.1.e: An object less dense than water floats partly submerged. An object that sits half submerged is floating too. An object with the same density as water stays suspended. An object denser than water sinks, and for it F<sub>b</sub> < W.
quiz.2.q: A cork with a volume of 200 cm³ and a density of 0.6 g/cm³ is tied to the bottom of a container by a string and is fully under water. If g = 10 m/s², what is the tension in the string, in N?
quiz.2.e: F<sub>b</sub> = 0.0002 · 1000 · 10 = 2 N and W = 0.12 kg · 10 = 1.2 N. The cork is in equilibrium, so F<sub>b</sub> = W + T. That gives T = 2 − 1.2 = 0.8 N.
quiz.3.q: The same object floats in liquid X with half its volume submerged, stays suspended in liquid Y, and sinks to the bottom in liquid Z. Which is true for the buoyant forces on the object?
quiz.3.e: For floating and suspended objects F<sub>b</sub> = W. In liquid Z, where the object sinks, F<sub>b</sub> < W.
quiz.3.y.0: For floating and suspended objects the buoyant force equals the weight, so F<sub>X</sub> and F<sub>Y</sub> must be equal.
quiz.3.y.1: How deep an object sits does not set the force by itself. For an object that sinks, the buoyant force is smaller than the weight.
quiz.3.y.3: For an object that sinks to the bottom, the buoyant force is smaller than the weight. Otherwise it would not sink.
A:ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Lower the stone into water, load the ship, and lift the balloon.
A:adimlar.0.metin: A 10 cm cube is under water. The water presses on it from every direction. The forces on the sides cancel each other. Look at the top and bottom faces.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Which face has the larger force on it?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The top face is closer to the surface of the water. Does pressure increase or decrease with depth?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The bottom face is deeper, and liquid pressure increases with depth. The push from below is 10 N larger than the push from above. This difference is the upward buoyant force (Fb).
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The sides are equal because they are at the same depth. The top and bottom faces are at different depths.
A:adimlar.1.metin: A stone hanging from a spring scale reads 5 N in air, and its volume is 200 cm³. Slowly lower the stone into the water until it is fully submerged. Then look at the reading.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: The reading dropped to 3 N. So F<sub>b</sub> = 5 − 3 = 2 N. Let us check: V<sub>sub</sub>·ρ<sub>liq</sub>·g = 0.0002 m³ × 1000 kg/m³ × 10 m/s² = 2 N.
A:adimlar.2.metin: The 10 cm cube from before is fully under water. Move it up and down. How do the forces on the top and bottom faces change?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: What happens to the buoyant force when you lower the fully submerged cube deeper?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: It is true that the pressures increase. But both increase together. Look at the difference.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Going deeper does not reduce the force on any face. Look at the difference.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The forces on both faces increase by the same amount, and the difference stays at 10 N. F<sub>b</sub> depends on the submerged volume, not on the depth.
A:adimlar.3.metin: You put a 1000 cm³ (6 N) wooden cube with a density of 0.6 g/cm³ into different liquids. Change the density of the liquid so that the cube floats exactly half submerged.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: Since 0.6 / 1.2 = 1/2, half of the cube is submerged. In every liquid where the cube floats, F<sub>b</sub> = W = 6 N. Only the submerged volume changes, and the object sinks less in a denser liquid.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Load containers onto the ship. Stop when the water reaches the load line on the hull (yellow circle).
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: Each container made the ship sit a little deeper. To balance the extra weight, the ship must displace more water. The load line shows how deep the ship can safely sit.
A:adimlar.5.metin: The volume of a submarine does not change, and when it is fully submerged F<sub>b</sub> is constant too. The submarine has taken seawater into its ballast tanks.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: What does a submarine do after taking water into its tanks?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The water entering the tanks makes the submarine heavier.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: A submarine changes its weight, not its volume. With water taken in, W > F<sub>b</sub> and the submarine dives. When the water is blown out with compressed air, W < F<sub>b</sub> and it rises. If W = F<sub>b</sub>, it stays suspended.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The volume, and so F<sub>b</sub>, stayed the same, but the weight increased.
A:adimlar.6.metin: 1 m³ of helium gets a buoyant force of about 12 N from the air, and its own weight is about 1.7 N. The basket and the balloon skin weigh 40 N. Make the balloon larger and lift it off the ground.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.tamam: At 4 m³, F<sub>b</sub> = 48 N, and the total weight is 40 + 6.8 = 46.8 N. So the balloon rises. Each m³ of helium gives a net lift of about 10 N.
A:kapanis.0: The buoyant force comes from a pressure difference. The bottom face is deeper, so it is pushed harder.
A:kapanis.1: By Archimedes' principle, Fb = Vsub·ρliq·g. The apparent weight equals W − Fb.
A:kapanis.2: Lowering a fully submerged object deeper does not change F<sub>b</sub>.
A:kapanis.3: For floating and suspended objects F<sub>b</sub> = W. For a floating object V<sub>sub</sub> / V = ρ<sub>obj</sub> / ρ<sub>liq</sub>.
A:kapanis.4: A ship floats by displacing a lot of water, a submarine dives by changing its weight, and a balloon flies on the buoyant force of the air.
